YOLOv3 formulates class prediction as a multilabel problem:  
• For each predicted bounding box, the network outputs one score per class using independent logistic (sigmoid) classifiers rather than a single softmax over all classes [YOLOv3.pdf, p.2].  
• During training, each class score is trained with a binary cross-entropy loss, treating each class prediction as a separate binary classification task [YOLOv3.pdf, p.2].  

Softmax is not used because it enforces that each box must belong to exactly one class, an assumption that breaks down in datasets with overlapping or non-mutually exclusive labels (for example, “Woman” and “Person” in Open Images). By using independent logistic classifiers, YOLOv3 can naturally model boxes that contain multiple, overlapping class labels without being constrained to a single choice [YOLOv3.pdf, p.2].

Darknet-53 is the convolutional backbone used in YOLOv3. It consists of 53 layers of alternating 3×3 and 1×1 convolutions with shortcut (residual) connections, making it substantially larger and more expressive than Darknet-19 while still being more efficient than deeper ResNets [YOLOv3.pdf, p.2].

Compared to ResNet-101 and ResNet-152 on ImageNet (256×256 single-crop):

• Accuracy  
  – Darknet-53 achieves 77.2% top-1 and 93.8% top-5 accuracy  
  – ResNet-101 achieves 77.1% top-1 and 93.7% top-5  
  – ResNet-152 achieves 77.6% top-1 and 93.8% top-5 [YOLOv3.pdf, p.3]

• Computational Cost  
  – Darknet-53 uses 18.7 billion operations  
  – ResNet-101 uses 19.7 billion  
  – ResNet-152 uses 29.4 billion [YOLOv3.pdf, p.3]

• GPU Utilization (BFLOP/s)  
  – Darknet-53: 1,457 GFLOP/s  
  – ResNet-101: 1,039 GFLOP/s  
  – ResNet-152: 1,090 GFLOP/s [YOLOv3.pdf, p.3]

• Inference Speed  
  – Darknet-53 runs at 78 FPS  
  – ResNet-101 runs at 53 FPS (Darknet-53 is ~1.5× faster)  
  – ResNet-152 runs at 37 FPS (Darknet-53 is ~2× faster) [YOLOv3.pdf, p.3]

Overall, Darknet-53 matches or betters the classification accuracy of ResNet-101/152 while using fewer operations, achieving higher FLOP‐rates, and running significantly faster on a Titan X GPU.

The two key additional improvements in YOLOv4—Mosaic augmentation and Self-Adversarial Training—are described as follows:

1. Mosaic Data Augmentation  
   • Instead of mixing only two images (as in CutMix), Mosaic randomly combines four different training images into one during each training iteration, providing four distinct contexts in a single sample [YOLOv4.pdf, p.6].  
   • This multi-image composition exposes the detector to objects appearing in novel surrounding contexts, improving its ability to generalize to objects outside their typical scenes [YOLOv4.pdf, p.6].  
   • Because each composite image contains four original images, the activation statistics for batch normalization are computed over four contexts per layer, effectively emulating a larger mini-batch and reducing the need for a physically large batch size [YOLOv4.pdf, p.6].

2. Self-Adversarial Training (SAT)  
   • SAT is a two-stage “adversarial” data augmentation technique where, in the first forward–backward pass, the network intentionally perturbs (attacks) the input image itself rather than its own weights, creating a modified image in which the target object is obscured or distorted [YOLOv4.pdf, p.6].  
   • In the second pass, the network is trained on this adversarially altered image to correctly detect the object despite the perturbation, thereby improving its robustness to challenging inputs [YOLOv4.pdf, p.6].

reference:
Mosaic represents a new data augmentation method that mixes 4 training images. Thus 4 different contexts are mixed, while CutMix mixes only 2 input images. This allows detection of objects outside their normal context. In addition, batch normalization calculates activation statistics from 4 different images on each layer. This significantly reduces the need for a large mini-batch size.
Self-Adversarial Training (SAT) also represents a new data augmentation technique that operates in 2 forward backward stages. In the 1st stage the neural network alters the original image instead of the network weights. In this way the neural network executes an adversarial attack on itself, altering the original image to create the deception that there is no desired object on the image. In the 2nd stage, the neural network is trained to detect an object on this modified image in the normal way.
CmBN represents a CBN modified version, defined as Cross mini-Batch Normalization (CmBN). This collects statistics only between mini-batches within a single batch.

Under the same testing environment (FP16-precision on NVIDIA Tesla T4 with TensorRT), YOLOv6 consistently outperforms other YOLO-series detectors in both speed (throughput and latency) and accuracy at various model scales:

• YOLOv6-N (input = 416×416) achieves 35.9% AP at 1,234 FPS, which is 7.9% higher AP than YOLOv5-N and 2.6% higher than YOLOv7-Tiny, while also delivering the best throughput and lowest latency among them [YOLOv6.pdf, p.1][YOLOv6.pdf, p.7].

• YOLOv6-T (input = 640×640) is 2.9% more accurate than YOLOv5-S and YOLOv7-Tiny at the same resolution, and runs 73 FPS faster than YOLOv5-S and 25 FPS faster than YOLOv7-Tiny (batch size = 1) [YOLOv6.pdf, p.7].  
• YOLOv6-M matches the speed of YOLOv5-M while improving AP by 4.2%; it also outperforms YOLOX-M and PPYOLOE-M by 2.7% and 0.6% AP, respectively, all at higher inference speed [YOLOv6.pdf, p.7].  
• YOLOv6-L delivers 2.8% and 1.1% higher AP than YOLOX-L and PPYOLOE-L under the same latency constraint. Its faster variant, YOLOv6-L-ReLU, reaches 51.7% AP with 8.8 ms latency, surpassing YOLOX-L, PPYOLOE-L, and YOLOv7 in both accuracy and speed [YOLOv6.pdf, p.7].

YOLO fundamentally departs from prior object detectors like DPM and R-CNN by collapsing the entire detection pipeline into a single convolutional network that is trained end-to-end.  Instead of:

•  Extracting hand-engineered or static features, running a separate region proposal or sliding-window search, classifying each candidate box with an SVM or region-specific classifier, and then post-processing those detections (as in DPM or R-CNN),  

YOLO  
•  Treats detection as a single regression problem: from raw pixels in the full image directly to bounding box coordinates and class probabilities in one pass. [YOLOv1.pdf, p.1]  
•  Embeds feature extraction, bounding box prediction, classification, and non-maximum suppression into one unified network that is trained jointly. [YOLOv1.pdf, p.4]  

Against R-CNN’s 2000 region proposals and multi-stage SVM pipeline or DPM’s sliding-window plus static features, YOLO’s grid-cell approach predicts only 98 boxes per image, constrains them spatially to reduce duplicates, and learns all parameters simultaneously. [YOLOv1.pdf, p.5]  

Primary advantage  
By unifying every step into a single model that can be optimized directly on detection loss, YOLO achieves real-time speeds (45 fps for the base model, 155 fps for Fast YOLO) while maintaining competitive accuracy, whereas DPM and R-CNN variants are orders of magnitude slower and require carefully tuned, multi-stage training. These complex pipelines are slow and difficult to optimize because each individual component must be trained separately. YOLO, on the other hand, reframes object detection as a single regression problem, predicting bounding box coordinates and class probabilities straight from image pixels. A single convolutional neural network evaluates the full image at once to predict multiple bounding boxes and their class probabilities simultaneously. The primary advantage of this unified architecture is that it is extremely fast, with the base YOLO model processing images in real-time at 45 frames per second, and Fast YOLO processing them at 155 frames per second.

The key distinction between “Bag of Freebies” (BoF) and “Bag of Specials” (BoS) in YOLO v4 is:

· Bag of Freebies (BoF) comprises techniques that only modify the training process—most often data-augmentation or regularization schemes—so that no additional cost is incurred at inference time [YOLOv4.pdf, p.3].  
· Bag of Specials (BoS) comprises architectural modules or operations (e.g. new activation functions, feature-aggregation blocks) that slightly increase inference complexity in exchange for higher accuracy [YOLOv4.pdf, p.7].

Among the BoF methods, two novel data-augmentation schemes introduced in YOLO v4 are:

1. CutMix: Randomly cut a rectangular patch from one image and paste it into another, then re-weight the two images’ labels in proportion to the area of the patch. This encourages the model to learn from partial object views and helps regularize against over-fitting [YOLOv4.pdf, p.3].  
2. Mosaic: Construct a single training sample by combining four different images into one in a 2×2 grid. By exposing objects at various scales and contexts within a single image, Mosaic significantly diversifies training data without incurring any inference overhead [YOLOv4.pdf, p.7].

'Bag of freebies' are methods that improve the object detector's accuracy without increasing the inference cost at all, typically by only altering the off-line training strategy or increasing training cost. In contrast, 'Bag of specials' are plugin modules or post-processing methods that do slightly increase the inference cost, but provide a significant improvement to accuracy by enhancing attributes like the receptive field or attention mechanisms.
The researchers introduced two new 'Bag of Freebies' data augmentation methods:
1. Mosaic: This method mixes four different training images together, allowing the model to learn to detect objects outside of their normal context. Because it processes four different images simultaneously on each layer, it also allows batch normalization to calculate activation statistics across a wider variety of inputs, significantly reducing the need for a large mini-batch size.
2. Self-Adversarial Training (SAT): This operates in two forward-backward stages. In the first stage, the neural network executes an adversarial attack on itself by altering the original image to deceive the network into thinking there is no desired object. In the second stage, the network is trained normally to detect the object on this newly modified image.

In YOLOv3, the center of each predicted box is computed per grid cell as  
 bx = sigmoid(tx) + Cx,  
 by = sigmoid(ty) + Cy,  
where Cx and Cy are the integer coordinates of the cell. Because sigmoid(tx)∈(0,1), placing a prediction very near a cell boundary (i.e. making bx approach Cx or Cx+1) requires tx to take on extremely large positive or negative values. This makes the model highly sensitive to the choice of grid and hampers learning and localization for objects that straddle cell borders. [YOLOv4.pdf, p.8]

YOLOv4 “eliminates grid sensitivity” by simply scaling the sigmoid output by a factor greater than 1.0. In practice this lets the network predict offsets outside the strict (0,1) range without needing extreme pre-sigmoid activations, thereby smoothing predictions across cell boundaries and removing the hard grid-imposed limits on box centers. [YOLOv4.pdf, p.8]

reference: In YOLOv3, the evaluation of object coordinates uses the equations bx = σ(tx) + cx and by = σ(ty) + cy, where cx and cy are strictly whole numbers. Because of how the sigmoid function (σ) works, the model requires extremely high absolute values for tx in order for the predicted coordinate bx to approach the whole numbers cx or cx + 1. This makes it very difficult for the model to detect objects that fall exactly on the grid boundaries. YOLOv4 solves this issue simply by multiplying the sigmoid by a factor exceeding 1.0. This adjustment eliminates the grid sensitivity effect, allowing the model to more easily predict coordinates that lie on the grid lines where an object would otherwise be undetectable.

This multilabel formulation removes the softmax’s one-class-per-box constraint, allowing a single box to be assigned multiple, potentially overlapping labels (e.g. Woman and Person), which is crucial for handling complex datasets like Open Images where classes frequently co-occur [YOLOv3.pdf, p.2].

reference: Instead of a softmax function, YOLOv3 uses independent logistic classifiers to perform multilabel classification. The developers made this change because a softmax function imposes the strict assumption that each bounding box contains exactly one class. This assumption fails in complex domains like the Open Images Dataset, which contains many overlapping labels, such as a single object being labeled as both 'Woman' and 'Person'. By using a multilabel approach with independent logistic classifiers, the system is much better equipped to model data where multiple classes can apply to the same box.

Darknet-53 vs. Darknet-19  
• Darknet-53 is a deeper, hybrid design that merges ideas from Darknet-19 with residual (shortcut) connections.  It still uses successive 3×3 and 1×1 convolutions, but expands from 19 to 53 convolutional layers and inserts shortcut paths throughout the network [YOLOv3.pdf, p.2].  
• This deeper architecture makes Darknet-53 “much more powerful” than Darknet-19 while retaining the same basic convolutional building blocks [YOLOv3.pdf, p.2].  

Efficiency compared to ResNet  
• On ImageNet classification (single-crop, 256×256), Darknet-53 achieves accuracy on par with state-of-the-art models but with substantially fewer floating-point operations and higher throughput [YOLOv3.pdf, p.2].  
• It outperforms ResNet-101 (in accuracy) while running 1.5× faster, and matches ResNet-152’s accuracy while running 2× faster [YOLOv3.pdf, p.2].  
• Darknet-53 also attains the highest measured FLOPs/sec among these networks, indicating superior GPU utilization and evaluation speed [YOLOv3.pdf, p.3].  

## Sources  
YOLOv3.pdf
reference: Darknet-53 acts as a hybrid between the Darknet-19 network used in YOLOv2 and modern residual networks. It still uses successive 3x3 and 1x1 convolutional layers, but it is significantly larger (53 layers) and now incorporates shortcut connections. Compared to competing models, Darknet-53 performs on par with state-of-the-art classifiers but with far more efficiency. It achieves better accuracy than ResNet-101 while being 1.5 times faster, and it matches the performance of ResNet-152 while being 2 times faster. The developers note that Darknet-53 better utilizes the GPU and achieves the highest measured floating-point operations per second, largely because ResNets possess 'way too many layers and aren't very efficient'.

YOLOv3 introduces multi-scale predictions—that is, it makes detection at three different feature-map resolutions—to boost its ability to localize small objects.  This change reverses YOLO’s historical weakness on small targets (it now has relatively high AP for small objects), but, unexpectedly, the model’s performance on medium and large objects degrades compared to its predecessors [YOLOv3.pdf, p.3].

YOLOv3.pdf
reference: YOLOv3 attempts to solve the small object problem by predicting boxes at three different scales, utilizing a concept similar to feature pyramid networks. The network takes a feature map, upsamples it by 2x, and concatenates it with a finer-grained feature map from earlier in the network. This allows the network to combine high-level semantic information with fine-grained details. Because of these new multi-scale predictions, YOLOv3 successfully reversed its historical weakness and now achieves relatively high performance on small objects. However, the unexpected trade-off is that YOLOv3 now exhibits comparatively worse performance when detecting medium and larger-sized objects.

Traditional MSE‐based regression treats each of the four bounding‐box parameters (e.g. x, y, w, h) as independent targets and penalizes them with an L2 (or L1) loss.  The YOLOv4 paper points out two main drawbacks of this approach:  
1. It ignores the fact that the four parameters jointly define a single, coherent box—i.e. it ignores the “integrity” of the object’s shape.  Treating them independently can lead to suboptimal placements even if each coordinate is close individually.  
2. Because L1/L2 losses on {x, y, w, h} scale with the magnitude of those values, larger boxes incur disproportionately larger losses, making optimization scale‐dependent.  (By contrast, the evaluation metric—IoU—is scale invariant.) [YOLOv4.pdf, p.3]

To address these issues, the paper adopts IoU-based losses that treat the box as a whole.  In particular, CIoU loss augments the basic IoU‐loss with two additional terms:  
• A penalty on the normalized distance between the centers of the predicted box and ground truth (encouraging better centering).  
• A penalty on aspect‐ratio differences (encouraging shape consistency).  

By jointly optimizing overlap area, center‐distance, and aspect ratio, CIoU yields a single, scale-invariant regression objective that respects the holistic geometry of the box, leading to faster convergence and higher localization accuracy. [YOLOv4.pdf, p.3]  

## Sources  
YOLOv4.pdf
reference: The paper notes that directly estimating coordinate values using MSE is problematic because it treats the points of the bounding box as independent variables, which fails to consider the integrity of the object itself. Additionally, when traditional methods calculate the l1 or l2 loss of a box, the loss inherently increases with the scale of the object. To process this better, researchers shifted to Intersection over Union (IoU) losses, which are scale-invariant. The YOLOv4 authors utilize CIoU loss because it simultaneously considers the overlapping area, the distance between the center points of the predicted and ground truth boxes, and the aspect ratio, leading to better convergence speed and accuracy on the bounding box regression problem.
